title: OrchestrateDASH agent manifest v2
description: Additive v2 manifest. It preserves the telemetry v1 fields and adds an Agent DOM declaration. Unknown fields remain forward-compatible. Credential values are forbidden; connection fields describe requirements only.

expected_interval_seconds.description: The longest gap DASH should expect between this agent's activity before treating it as stalled rather than quietly idle. Optional and meaningful only alongside type "schedule": schedule is free text ("weekdays at 08:00 local time") and DASH does not parse it, so an absent value means no expectation can be derived and this agent is never marked stalled.

task_inputs.description: What files this agent accepts as a task, declared per role (MAR-434). Optional, and absent means the agent takes no files — which is every agent shipped before this block existed, so absence must never be read as an unrestricted agent. The declaration is what the runner narrows its own ceilings down to; it can never widen them, so a manifest asking for a 4 GiB input gets the runner's limit and a refusal, not 4 GiB. See runner/workspace.ts effectiveLimits.

taskInputRole.description:
One kind of file a task accepts, in the user's vocabulary (MAR-434).

A role rather than a slot number, because the surface says "Customer brief" and "Price list" and a person selects against those words. `id` is what a command carries and never what a person reads — the split `permissionGrant` already makes, for the same reason.

**Media types are checked against sniffed bytes, not against the extension.** An extension is a claim by whoever named the file; `runner/workspace.ts` reads the first bytes and refuses a mismatch. So declaring `application/pdf` here means the runner will refuse a renamed executable, and declaring nothing means the runner does not narrow — which is honest but is not the same as accepting anything, because the runner's own ceilings still apply.

id.description: Technical vocabulary, e.g. `customer_brief`. Carried in commands; never rendered on a guided surface.

label.description: What a person reads, e.g. "Customer brief". Held to lib/copy/identifiers.ts.

description.description: Why this agent wants it. Rendered beside the file picker so a person can tell whether they are handing over the right document.

required.description: Whether the task can start without it. Required rather than optional in the schema because a renderer that has to guess would guess `false` and let a task start missing the file it exists to read.

max_count.description: The runner lowers this to its own ceiling and never raises it.

media_types.description: Accepted types as the runner sniffs them, e.g. `application/pdf`. Absent means the runner does not narrow by type. Note that DASH does not open a ZIP container to tell a .docx from a .xlsx, so both are `application/zip` — declaring one and not the other narrows nothing.

max_file_bytes.description: Per file. Lowered to the runner's ceiling, never raised past it.

max_total_bytes.description: Across every file in this role. Lowered to the runner's ceiling, never raised past it.

panel.description:
The agent's own panel, declared rather than programmed (ADR 0008, MAR-552).

A panel is **data over a closed vocabulary** that DASH renders with its own trusted components. Agent-authored code never executes in DASH's renderer, and this block is not an escape hatch from that: what a panel can make DASH draw is one closed union, readable in `$defs.panelSectionV1` in a single sitting.

The absences are the argument. **No component takes a URL. No component takes markup. No component takes a path. No component takes an image. No component names another agent. No component asks the user for anything, and no event vocabulary exists.** Widening any of those means widening a pinned union in a reviewed commit, which is the by-value-pin discipline doing its job.

Optional, and **omitted when undeclared — never an empty object**, the exact rule `task_inputs` shipped with. Absence means the author declared no panel; it must never be read as "render something anyway".

panel_version.description: Which vocabulary the sections are written in. Version 1 is the closed five-component set below. See the if/then/else: a version DASH knows is checked strictly, a version it does not know is accepted structurally and rendered as one stated card.

title.description: What the author calls this panel. Rendered as a text node inside a region DASH itself heads, so it reads as the author's words and cannot be mistaken for a DASH verdict. Held to lib/copy/identifiers.ts.

sections.description: In render order. Bounded here rather than defended against in the renderer: a spec that cannot describe an unbounded render is better than a renderer that has to survive one.

panelSectionV1.description:
One section of a version 1 panel. The `type` enum is closed on purpose: a typo'd type is refused at import, loudly, rather than silently dropped at render — a half-drawn panel is a guess rendered as a fact.

Each branch of the oneOf below is discriminated by `type`, so a section matches exactly one shape and the renderer can narrow on the same field the author wrote.

id.description: Technical vocabulary, e.g. `latest_digest`. Travels so a section can be addressed; never rendered, the same split `taskInputRole.id` and `permissionGrant.id` already make.

label.description: What a person reads at the head of the section. Held to lib/copy/identifiers.ts.

type.description: The closed vocabulary, complete in this one array. `report` is the newest artifact of a role; `outputs` is the artifact cards filtered by role; `table` is rows from the newest JSON artifact of a role; `metrics` is labelled values from an artifact field or from a fact DASH itself observes; `note` is a bounded block of the author's own copy.

oneOf.description: report — the newest artifact of the named role, rendered through the artifact-card and digest machinery the run detail page already uses, receipt included.
outputs — the existing Outputs area, placeable and scopeable by the author. An absent `artifact_role` means every role this agent produced, which is what the Outputs area already shows.

table — rows from the newest JSON artifact of `source_role` whose body is an array of objects. A cell is an own-property lookup by `key`, rendered per `kind`; a value that is not the declared kind renders as absent, never coerced. There is deliberately no path or expression syntax: a path language is an interpreter, and interpreters grow.

key.description: One own property of a row object. An alphabet that cannot spell a separator, a traversal or a URL.

kind.description: How the cell is rendered. A value of a different kind renders as absent rather than being coerced, because a coerced cell is DASH asserting something the agent did not say.

oneOf.description: metrics — labelled values from either a top-level field of a JSON artifact or from the closed set of facts DASH itself observes. The two sources render differently attributed: an artifact field is *the agent's report*, a dash fact is *DASH's record*. Collapsing that distinction would let an agent's own number wear DASH's voice — it is `stated_at`/`received_at`'s split, applied to a number.
The agent's own report: one top-level field of the newest JSON artifact of this role.
DASH's own record. A closed set, each member already computed for an existing view — nothing here asks DASH to derive something new on an agent's behalf.

note — a bounded block of author copy, with the same standing as the manifest's `goal`: the author's words, rendered as the author's words, inside a region DASH heads as the author's own panel. An author can still be wrong in a note; the mitigation is attribution, not censorship, and DASH's verdict surfaces render outside the panel where no section can imitate them.

panelSectionOpaque.description:
A section of a panel version DASH does not know (ADR 0008).

Checked for structure only, so the document is accepted rather than rejected — the contract's additive-versioning rule, which lib/contracts.ts states as "DASH ignores what it does not understand rather than rejecting the document". DASH renders such a panel as **one stated card** saying the author declared it in a newer format, never section by section: a partially drawn panel is a guess presented as a fact.

`type` is an open string here precisely because the closed enum belongs to version 1 and must not rot into leniency to accommodate a version that has not been designed yet.

roleName.description: An artifact role, e.g. `digest`. Bindings name roles and never locations — MAR-507's rule ("the renderer names a kind of file and never a file") applied to data binding. The alphabet cannot spell a separator, a traversal or a URL, and the binding carries no agent, so a panel resolves roles against *this* agent's runs and cannot reach another's.

permissions.description:
What the agent declares it may do that needs no credential — the case `connections` cannot express, because every connection requirement carries an owner, fields and a validation action. Additive and optional: a manifest without this block declares nothing, which is different from declaring nothing is needed.

The shape deliberately mirrors the OrchestrateKit registry's component `permissions` block (read / write / approval_required_for) so a scaffolded manifest and an exported build brief describe a permission the same way. A second vocabulary here would mean the two documents could disagree about the same grant.

**This is a declaration, not a boundary.** The runner strips the environment (`runner/supervisor.ts`) but spawns an ordinary child process with unrestricted network access. DASH renders what the agent claims and who to ask about it; it does not enforce it, and no copy built on this block may say that it does. The same honesty ADR 0002 requires of the draft-only Gmail boundary applies here.

id.description: The registry's own name for the capability, e.g. `network`. Technical vocabulary: a guided surface renders `label`, never this.

label.description: What it may do, in the words a person reads. Held to lib/copy/identifiers.ts.

detail.description: The scope of the grant in plain language — what is included and what is not.
